chunks: Specifying discrete transistors for a drive. The question: If you're designing a motor/solenoid drive with discrete components, how do you spec your transistors?
Picking a separate (discrete) power transistor means working from the circuit to the datasheet.
The voltage rating must survive the supply plus the spike when the coil switches off. The current rating comes from stall or the current limit, but what really limits it is heat.
That depends on its on-resistance, R DS(on) , at your real gate voltage and temperature.
Think of choosing a rope to hang a load. It must survive the jerk when the load drops, not just the still weight: that is the voltage rating against the spike.
A rope rated at room temperature may weaken in a hot shed, just as R DS(on) rises when hot.
And a strong rope can be too stiff for your pulley: a transistor whose gate your driver cannot charge quickly.
The specification chain. Each datasheet number answers a specific question about the circuit; the end is a bench test that closes the loop.
MOSFET: the usual power transistor. Its gate is the control pin. When on, it acts as a small resistance. Voltage rating: the most voltage the switch can block when off.
Logic-level MOSFET: one that turns fully on from a low gate voltage, such as 2. 5 volts or 4. 5 volts, so a microcontroller can drive it.
Gate charge: the charge the driver must push into the gate to switch it. More charge means slower switching. Thermal resistance: degrees of warming per watt of loss.
A 12 volts motor runs at 5 amps (rms, the heating-equivalent value), with a 15 amps stall limit. A flyback diode holds turn-off spikes to 12.
7 volts, so a 40 volts logic-level MOSFET has plenty of margin.
If it has 10 milliohms at 25 degrees Celsius, it has about 16 milliohms hot, so conduction loss is 5 squared times 0. 016 equals 0. 4 watts.
Switching loss at 20 kilohertz is only about 0. 06 watts. With 50 degrees Celsius/W of thermal resistance, that adds about 23 degrees Celsius over the surroundings.
That is the whole idea: derive the part from the circuit.
"Voltage: at least twice the supply plus clamp, e. g. 40 volts on a 12 volts rail.
Current: size from stall or the current limit, but the real limit is heat, so use hot R DS(on) at my actual gate voltage, which means logic-level for 3.
3 or 5 volts drive, and compute I to the 2R plus switching and gate loss against thermal resistance.
Then gate charge and the Q gd over Q gs ratio for drive and Miller immunity, SOA or avalanche if unclamped, and the body diode for bridges."
